parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Describe how the piezoelectric crystal in a transducer generates ultrasound waves for use in medical diagnosis.

markscheme_points.text: alternating p.d. (applied to crystal) makes crystal vibrate
when frequency of applied p.d. equals natural frequency of crystal, crystal resonates
natural frequency of crystal is in ultrasound range

hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling the piezoelectric property - what happens to the shape or thickness of the crystal when a p.d. is applied across it?
Hint 2: To make the crystal vibrate continuously to emit a wave, what type of p.d. must you apply so the crystal is repeatedly stretched and compressed?
Hint 3: Think about when the vibration amplitude becomes very large and what value the crystal is cut to have for its natural frequency for medical use.
parts.proper_answer: An alternating p.d. applied to the crystal causes it to vibrate. When the frequency of the applied p.d. equals the natural frequency of vibration of the crystal, resonance occurs with large amplitude. The crystal is cut so its natural frequency is in the ultrasound range.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Piezoelectric Response**
Think of the crystal sitting with electrodes on opposite faces. When you apply a p.d., the crystal changes shape - it expands or contracts slightly. Reverse the p.d. and it does the opposite. This is the piezoelectric effect working in reverse.

Step 2: **Driving Continuous Vibration**
Now apply an alternating p.d.: $$V = V_0 \sin(2\pi f t)$$ The electric field reverses millions of times per second, so the crystal is forced to expand and contract at frequency $f$. Each vibrating face pushes on the surrounding medium and emits a longitudinal pressure wave.

Step 3: **Using Resonance for Ultrasound**
You get a very large amplitude vibration when you drive at resonance, that is when $$f_{applied} = f_{natural}$$ of the crystal. The crystal thickness is chosen so that $f_{natural}$ is in the ultrasound region, typically a few MHz, well above $20\text{ kHz}$, suitable for medical diagnosis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A parallel ultrasound beam is incident on the boundary between two media, as illustrated in Fig. 10.1.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

The media have specific acoustic impedances $Z_1$ and $Z_2$.

At the boundary, a fraction $\alpha$ of the incident intensity of the ultrasound beam is reflected. The remainder is transmitted.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by specific acoustic impedance.

markscheme_points.text: speed is speed of ultrasound in medium (and density of medium)

hints: Hint 1: Specific acoustic impedance is a property of the medium itself, not of the wave intensity. Which two properties of the medium control how easily sound travels through it?
Hint 2: Recall how $Z$ combines a mass-per-volume term with a wave-speed term as a simple product.
parts.proper_answer: Specific acoustic impedance $Z = \rho c$, where $\rho$ is the density of the medium and $c$ is the speed of ultrasound in the medium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Z Tells You**
$Z$ measures how much a medium resists the passage of ultrasound. A dense, stiff medium with fast wave speed has high impedance. It is defined for each medium separately.

Step 2: **The Definition**
In symbols: $$Z = \rho c$$ where $\rho$ is the density of the medium in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$ and $c$ is the speed of ultrasound in that medium in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. So $Z$ has unit $\text{kg m}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Describe how $\alpha$ depends on the relative values of $Z_1$ and $Z_2$.

markscheme_points.text: (α is close to) 0 when Z1 and Z2 are equal
(α is close to) 1 when Z1 and Z2 are very different

hints: Hint 1: Think of the two extreme cases - a wave staying in almost the same material versus hitting a very different material like soft tissue to air.
Hint 2: Link the fraction reflected $\alpha$ to the size of the mismatch between $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ - when is $\alpha$ near zero and when near one?
parts.proper_answer: $\alpha$ is close to 0 when $Z_1$ is approximately equal to $Z_2$, with almost full transmission. $\alpha$ is close to 1 when $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are very different, with almost full reflection.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Matched Impedances**
If $Z_1 \approx Z_2$, the wave sees almost no change at the boundary. There is almost no reflection, so the reflected fraction $$\alpha \approx 0$$ and most intensity is transmitted. This is why coupling gel is used to match impedances.

Step 2: **Large Mismatch**
If $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are very different, the boundary is a large obstacle. Most of the wave cannot enter the second medium and is reflected back, so $$\alpha \approx 1$$ A common misconception is that large $Z$ alone gives large reflection - it is the difference between $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ that matters.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A parallel ultrasound beam of intensity $I_0$ enters a region of soft tissue. After passing a distance of $2.1\text{ cm}$ through this tissue, the intensity of the ultrasound is $0.62I_0$.

Calculate the linear attenuation coefficient $\mu$ of ultrasound in the soft tissue. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: Intensity in tissue does not fall linearly with distance. What type of exponential drop describes absorption and scattering of a parallel beam?
Hint 2: Take natural logs of both sides to isolate $\mu$ using $I = 0.62I_0$ and $x = 2.1\text{ cm}$, and keep $x$ in cm to get $\mu$ in $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Attenuation Law**
For a parallel beam, intensity falls exponentially with distance in the medium: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ where $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient and $x$ is the distance travelled. Here $I/I_0 = 0.62$ and $x = 2.1\text{ cm}$.

Step 2: **Solve for mu**
Take natural logs: $$\ln\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right) = -\mu x$$ $$\ln(0.62) = -\mu \times 2.1$$ $$\mu = -\frac{\ln(0.62)}{2.1} = \frac{0.478}{2.1} \approx 0.23\text{ cm}^{-1}$$ The unit is inverse length, here $\text{cm}^{-1}$ because $x$ was in cm, equivalent to about $23\text{ m}^{-1}$.
